source_review.notes: Reviewed all twelve references for identity, edition, date, and scope. The official ISO record confirms ISO/IEC/IEEE 42020:2019 as published, confirmed in January 2025, and marked to be revised in January 2026 with a successor work item under development; the chapter states this status without claiming the current edition withdrawn. Publisher and official records confirmed ISO 42010:2022, Ozkaya, Building Evolutionary Architectures second edition, Continuous Delivery, and Software Architecture in Practice fourth edition. SEI and IEEE records confirm the 2022 Sangwan-Negahban-Nord-Ozkaya release-planning article and the 2016 Architecture Options Workshop paper. IEEE/ACM records confirm the Nord-Ozkaya-Kruchten, Boehm, and Parnas papers. Fowler's evolutionary-architecture foreword was checked on 2026-09-06.

evidence: Reviewed increment set, hard prerequisite relation, graph, release assignment, effort, release capacity, state invariants, value, gates, transition-component set, expiry, and fact authority before use.
Checked directed-edge relation, strict release inequality, indexed capacity sum, ceiling lower bound, finite product concepts, and set membership for consistent units and scope.
Confirmed dependencies requiring same atomic release are excluded from the strict earlier-release relation and require an explicit model.
notation_and_syntax.notes: Graph feasibility, capacity, value, authority, and evidence are separate obligations rather than one optimization score.

evidence: Executed the capacity scheduler and independently confirmed Release 1 observe plus platform effort 3, Release 2 seam effort 2, Release 3 contract plus data-copy effort 3, Release 4 cutover effort 1, and Release 5 retire effort 2.
Recomputed Exercise 2 total effort as 12 and workload-only lower bound ceiling(12/5)=3 releases.
Confirmed the strict 2-to-4-to-1 dependency chain requires three distinct release indices even though its effort totals 7.
numerical_recomputation.notes: Effort units and capacities are hypothetical and not presented as duration estimates.

evidence: Reviewed both directions of the finite topological-order theorem: a directed cycle contradicts strict precedence, while repeated removal of an indegree-zero vertex constructs an order for an acyclic graph.
Verified total-effort divided by capacity is a lower bound only when dependencies and indivisibility are ignored, so adding constraints cannot reduce the modeled release count.
Verified every active transition component requires an owner and expiry or must be reclassified and funded as durable architecture.
symbolic_recomputation.notes: The theorem proves feasibility for the declared graph, not roadmap quality or optimality.

evidence: Reviewed dependency cycles, oversized work, same-release atomicity, specialized resources, unavailable evidence, incompatible versions, unbounded fleet skew, dual authority, irreversible state, and supplier delay.
Reviewed emergency debt, sunk cost, false precision, speculative platforms, missing retirement, simultaneous transitions, sparse metrics, operation load, and recovery gaps.
Reviewed public transit, safety, accessibility, fare, labor, procurement, privacy, jurisdiction, emergency, offline, agency, and affected-user authority limits.
boundary_and_adversarial_cases.notes: Rolling-wave flexibility is bounded by durable outcomes and hard invariants.

evidence: Traced operable release states, hard constraints, real prerequisites, single authority, mixed-version compatibility, governed temporary components, full-lifecycle capacity, visible uncertainty, decision history, retirement, and outcome evidence across the planning method.
Confirmed each release state includes behavior, data, versions, operations, recovery, security, and support rather than a task list alone.
Confirmed architecture increments and enablers have consumers, acceptance evidence, and stopping or removal conditions.
invariant_checking.notes: Activation without contraction and retirement is explicitly incomplete.

evidence: Reviewed the topological theorem for finiteness, strict precedence, indegree-zero existence, and induction premises.
Reviewed the capacity lower-bound argument for constant compatible capacity and its exclusion of skill, gate, and dependency constraints.
Reviewed the feature-first versus architecture-first counterexample to ensure neither ordering is claimed to dominate universally.
proof_review.notes: All proofs and counterexamples support bounded planning claims only.

evidence: Audited uses of theorem, feasible, necessary, sufficient, optimal, proof, authority, runway, complete, safe, value, debt, current, and validated for scope and assumptions.
Confirmed a topological order, greedy schedule, target diagram, metric, prototype, deployment, and supplier promise are each denied stronger conclusions than they support.
Confirmed public-transit architecture evidence is not presented as transport, safety, accessibility, labor, fare, privacy, or procurement approval.
proof_sketch_labeling.notes: No internal review or planning model is mislabeled as external validation.

The chapter supplies actionable state, dependency, capacity, checkpoint, and evidence practices. Internal practitioner-oriented review only.

pedagogical_review.notes: Verified graduate and professional multi-release planning depth, a formal prerequisite and capacity model, topological theorem, executable release schedule, five named invariants, eighteen distinct misconceptions, ten varied worked examples with explicit conclusions, and five progressive exercises with complete answers ending in an unfamiliar regional-transit transfer.

limitations: Internal evidence record only; no external academic or practitioner review is claimed. Source checks, structural validation, graph proofs, capacity arithmetic, hypothetical cases, and one local Python execution do not validate an external roadmap, prove estimates or value, establish resource interchangeability, guarantee delivery, compatibility, recovery, authority, or retirement, or provide transport, safety, accessibility, fare, labor, procurement, privacy, legal, financial, security, policy, or regulatory approval.
